newsitem.title: USA: Clinton calls for aid to gang victims.
newsitem.headline: Clinton calls for aid to gang victims.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Saturday urged states to earmark $44 million from a federal crime fund to help pay the costs for victims of gang violence.

As Clinton took a one-day break from the campaign trail to celebrate his wife Hillary's 49th birthday, a daily tracking poll taken for Reuters showed his lead over Republican Bob Dole increasing, while third party candidate Ross Perot was generating new support.
Clinton used his weekly radio address to say the nation needed to "stand up for the rights and interests of crime victims."

"As we prevent crime and punish criminals, we must also always remember the victims of crime themselves," Clinton said. "When you're a victim, especially a victim of violent crime, the losses you face go far beyond the money stolen or the property destroyed."
"We must do everything we can to help the victims of crime to make sure their voices are heard in the corridors of justice," Clinton said.
"We're putting crime victims where they belong, at the center of the criminal justice system, not on the outside looking in," he said.

Under the Justice Department's Crime Victims Fund, money from fines, penalty assessments and bond forfeitures paid for federal crimes is distributed to states to compensate victims for such costs such as unpaid medical bills, mental health counseling, funeral expenses and lost wages.
The money also goes to public and non-profit organizations that help victims. No taxpayer money is involved.
Because of the successful prosecution of several large cases, the fund has grown by more than 250 percent in the last four years.

Last year, Japan's Daiwa Bank paid a fine of $340 million fine to the fund to settle a criminal fraud case stemming from illegal trading activity in New York. This month, the Archer Daniels Midland Co. paid a $100 million anti-trust fine.
Clinton proposed that states use 10 percent of the $440 million from those two cases and direct it toward victims of gang violence, an increasing problem in America.

Noting that some of the funds already have been targeted to specific cases, such as the victims of domestic violence, rape or child abuse, Clinton said there would be "another key priority as well. Violent juvenile gangs can leave broken bodies and ruin neighborhoods in their wake."
He said children aged 12 to 15 are the most likely victims of gang violence but that they often are afraid to testify because they face the wrath of an entire gang.

He suggested some money could go to organizations like Teens on Target in Los Angeles and Oakland, Calif., which help gang victims, many of them disabled, speak to thousands of youngsters each year to warn about the dangers of gang life.
"We can teach our children right from wrong and keep them from following a path that only leads to a life of crime, disappointment and destruction," he said.

Clinton outlined the proposal a day after making a two-day campaign swing through his native South during which he underscored his crime-fighting credentials. He embarks on a three-day tour of seven states on Sunday.

The president and Mrs Clinton, who also interrupted a hectic campaign schedule, observed a private low-key celebration of her birthday. One aide said the biggest treat for her "was a chance just to sleep in."

On Saturday, Clinton led Dole by 46.7 percent to 33.6 percent in the Reuters poll conducted by John Zogby Group International. Reform Party candidate Perot's support was 7.8 percent, up from 6 percent on Friday. There were 10.1 percent undecided.
